entry.title: The Claude and Codex you already pay for, on a map
entry.summary: Vibisual is a desktop app that runs the Claude Code and Codex you already use. Agents become bubbles, several of them share one screen, and the conveniences a terminal never had sit on top.
entry.content:
Vibisual is a desktop app. You install it, a window opens, and inside it you use the Claude Code and Codex you are already subscribed to. There is no new account to make and no API key to paste. The app runs the CLI that is installed on your machine, so the plan and the login you use in the terminal carry straight over.

What changes is the screen. Right-click the empty canvas, pick a Claude agent or a Codex agent from the menu, and a bubble appears where you clicked. One bubble is one agent. Right-click again and there is another. Instead of keeping several terminal tabs open and remembering which one is doing what, you lay the agents out on one screen and look at them.

Double-click a bubble and that agent's workspace opens in the same window: the conversation, a file tree, a code editor, diffs and a terminal, all in one place. You type what you want and run it. If you do not like what the agent did, you fix it right there instead of switching to another program.

When an agent wants to write a file, it stops at an approval card. The card shows the exact path and the content. You allow it once, allow it for the session, or deny it with a reason the agent will read.

Close the workspace and the run shows up as a map. Every file the agent reads or edits appears as a bubble next to its folder, with an edge back to the agent that touched it. You no longer scroll back through a log to find out how far it got. A button at the bottom-left hides the file bubbles or brings them back, and the heatmap colours the files that were read most, or written most.

Agents are not the only thing you can place. The same right-click menu has All Model, which drops a bubble for a model running on your own machine, so Claude, Codex and a local model sit side by side on one canvas. When you want to type commands yourself, place a terminal bubble. When you want a screen or a program window kept in view, place a capture bubble.

The small things you need while working are in there too. Pin a sticky memo next to a conversation and it is still there when you open that session again. The memo app lives on the canvas as a bubble you double-click to open. Commands and prompts you use often go on the script shelf, one click away.

Two questions come up as soon as you run several agents, and both are answered at a glance. The ring in the header is plan usage: how much of the five-hour and weekly limits is gone, with Claude and Codex on separate tabs. Command Center gathers every session in the project into one window, with the ones waiting for your answer at the top.

The video above fits part of this into 1 minute 41 seconds. A Claude agent builds a coupon feature, and a Codex agent writes the tests for it.

Vibisual is free, and the source is open under Apache-2.0. It runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, with no account, entirely on your own machine. It needs the Claude CLI installed; Codex is only for those who want it. This is still an early version and there are rough edges. The installer is on the releases page.

entry.title: 0.1.14: the update button actually updates
entry.summary: Pressing Update closed the app and brought it back on the same version. Three fixes, all about the moments around shutdown.
entry.content:
The installer was launched before the app had finished shutting down. It replaces the installed files by renaming them one at a time, and that fails outright while Vibisual.exe is still running — after five one-second retries it gave up and installed nothing. From your side the app simply closed and came back on the old version. The installer is now launched at the very last moment, once cleanup is done and the process is about to disappear.

Shutdown itself was the other half of the problem. It waited for every open network connection to finish on its own, so a phone still connected over LAN access, or an idle keep-alive socket, could hold the app open for over a minute — 68 seconds, measured. Sockets are now cut once we have decided to close, and cleanup has a hard four-second ceiling after which the app exits regardless. Everything written to disk is flushed before that point.

The update button no longer asks twice, either. It already warns you and asks for confirmation; the ordinary close-confirmation was then asking again about the same thing — and the time spent answering it was enough for the installer to give up.

entry.title: Why we drew the terminal as space
entry.summary: A log tells you what happened, in order. A map tells you where everything is, right now. Agent runs need the second one.
entry.content:
A terminal is a good instrument for one worker. One cursor, one column of output, time running downward. When you were the one typing, that shape matched the work exactly.

Five agents break it. Output from unrelated tasks interleaves, the thing you care about scrolls away while you read something else, and the question you actually have — which one is stuck? — gets answered only by paging back through text that has already moved.

So we stopped printing the run and started drawing it. A node per agent, an edge per handoff, a child bubble per tool call. Position carries meaning, and state is a colour instead of a sentence you have to find.

The surprising part was not the map. It was that the same canvas turned out to be the right place to design the team: if a graph is how you read a run, a graph is also how you write one. Configuration and observation ended up being the same picture, seen at two different times.

entry.title: Designing a five-agent checkout refactor
entry.summary: One orchestrator, a schema migration, an API rewrite, a test runner that may not write, and a doc writer that waits for green.
entry.content:
Take a checkout refactor touching a migration, two route files and a price helper. Done by one agent it is a long single session, and one mistake anywhere costs the whole run.

Split five ways it becomes a graph. The orchestrator owns the plan. schema-migrator writes the migration in its own worktree and hands the new column names forward. api-builder rewrites the route against them.

test-runner gets read-only access to src/** — it can run the suite and read anything, but it cannot fix what it finds. That constraint is the point: a runner that edits code stops being a measurement.

doc-writer sits behind an edge from test-runner and starts only when the suite is green, so the changelog never describes a build that got rolled back. The whole design is five bubbles and five edges, and it reads faster than the paragraph describing it.
